package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via exploit payloads and shell scripts, not a traditional package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (affects multiple Linux/IoT device firmware versions via CVEs)
package_info.why_malicious: The IZ1H9 malware is a Mirai-based botnet variant that targets Linux-based IoT and network devices by exploiting a wide range of known vulnerabilities. It achieves initial compromise by delivering and executing malicious shell scripts, which in turn download and run architecture-specific bot binaries. The malware deletes system and temporary logs to evade detection, modifies firewall rules to block administrative access and maintain persistence, and establishes outbound connections to hardcoded command-and-control (C2) servers. Its primary objective is to conscript compromised devices into a botnet for use in large-scale DDoS and brute-force attacks, while employing anti-forensics and propagation techniques to maximize reach and resilience.

execution_context.trigger: exploit-triggered (remote code execution via HTTP request to vulnerable web interface parameters)
execution_context.file_location: Injected via vulnerable web interface parameters (e.g., tools_ip_url, key, etc.)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon exploit-triggered remote code execution, the code issues an outbound HTTP request to download a shell script from an external server, pipes the script directly to the shell for execution, and initiates the malware installation process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This command enables arbitrary code execution by downloading and immediately executing a remote shell script from an untrusted IP address, a classic initial access and malware delivery technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Device web interfaces should never allow arbitrary command execution or the download and execution of remote scripts without strict authentication and validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update mechanisms may download and execute scripts, but only from authenticated, trusted sources and with explicit user or administrator consent.
key_indicators: Direct download and execution of remote shell script via HTTP
Use of raw IP address instead of domain to evade DNS-based blocklists
Absence of integrity or authenticity verification for downloaded code
Execution of downloaded code in the current shell context

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after initial infection via l.sh execution)
execution_context.file_location: l.sh (downloaded shell script, typically in /tmp or other writable directory)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, immediately after infection, the code recursively deletes all files in system log and temporary directories, erasing evidence of compromise and impeding forensic analysis.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Indiscriminate deletion of log and temporary files is a well-known anti-forensics tactic used by malware to conceal its presence and hinder incident response.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate scripts should not erase system logs or temporary files without explicit user or administrator approval, especially not immediately after code execution.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Log rotation or cleanup scripts may remove old logs, but such actions are scheduled, selective, and never occur immediately after arbitrary code execution.
key_indicators: Immediate and recursive deletion of /var/log/*, /tmp/*, and /var/tmp/*
Log deletion occurring directly after infection or script execution
Targeting of multiple standard log and temp directories

execution_context.trigger: runtime (as part of l.sh execution after initial infection)
execution_context.file_location: l.sh (downloaded shell script, typically in /tmp or other writable directory)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script downloads an architecture-specific Mirai bot binary from a remote server, sets executable permissions on the binary, and launches it in the background, enrolling the device into the botnet.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Fetching and executing architecture-specific binaries from an untrusted external source is a hallmark of botnet propagation and device compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate device scripts should only download and execute binaries from trusted vendors, with cryptographic verification and user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Firmware updates may involve downloading and running binaries, but only from authenticated, trusted sources and with integrity checks.
key_indicators: Download of architecture-specific binary (e.g., bot.arm7) from external IP
Setting executable permissions on unknown binary
Background execution of newly downloaded binary

execution_context.trigger: runtime (as part of l.sh execution after bot binary deployment)
execution_context.file_location: l.sh (downloaded shell script, typically in /tmp or other writable directory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j DROP; iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 23 -j DROP; ...
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the script modifies the device's firewall rules by adding iptables rules to block incoming connections on administrative ports such as SSH (22) and Telnet (23), preventing legitimate access and remediation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated modification of firewall rules to block remote management ports is a common persistence and anti-remediation tactic used by malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Firewall changes should be performed only by authorized administrators, not by scripts executed via remote exploits or without user knowledge.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Firewall configuration is legitimate when performed by authorized users for security hardening, not by untrusted scripts.
key_indicators: Automated addition of iptables rules targeting SSH and Telnet ports
Blocking of remote management and administrative access
Firewall manipulation performed by malware-controlled script

execution_context.trigger: runtime (after infection, as part of bot binary execution)
execution_context.file_location: Mirai bot binary (e.g., bot.arm7, executed from /tmp or similar directory)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after infection, the bot binary establishes an outbound TCP connection to a hardcoded C2 server IP and port, sends a check-in message, and waits to receive further instructions for DDoS or brute-force attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited outbound connections to hardcoded IP addresses for command and control are a primary indicator of botnet malware activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate device software should not connect to unknown external servers for instructions, especially using hardcoded IPs and custom protocols.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IoT devices may connect to vendor cloud services, but such connections use documented endpoints and secure protocols, not hardcoded, unlisted IPs.
key_indicators: Outbound connection to hardcoded C2 IP (194.180.48.101) on non-standard port (5034)
Waiting for binary or protocol-specific response from C2

execution_context.trigger: runtime (as part of bot binary execution after C2 check-in)
execution_context.file_location: Mirai bot binary (data section, executed in memory)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: preset_login_credentials = xor_decode(data_section, key=0x54); for cred in preset_login_credentials: try_bruteforce(cred);
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after C2 check-in, the bot binary decodes an embedded XOR-encoded list of default credentials from its data section and systematically attempts to brute-force logins on other devices over the network, enabling lateral movement and further propagation.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Embedding and decoding credential lists for automated brute-force attacks is a classic worm and botnet propagation technique, enabling the malware to spread autonomously.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should never attempt to brute-force logins on other devices or contain encoded credential lists for unauthorized access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may use similar techniques, but only in authorized, controlled environments with explicit permission.
key_indicators: Presence of XOR-encoded credential lists in binary data section
Automated brute-force login attempts using decoded credentials
Network scanning and propagation logic embedded in bot binary

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits a remote code execution vulnerability on a target device via a crafted HTTP request to vulnerable web interface parameters.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial infection and execution of remote shell script.

attack_chain.action: Shell script (l.sh) deletes system and temporary logs to cover tracks and hinder forensic analysis.
Shell script downloads and executes architecture-specific Mirai bot binaries from an external server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device is enrolled into the botnet.

attack_chain.action: Shell script modifies firewall rules to block administrative access and prevent remediation.
Bot binary connects to hardcoded C2 server, sends check-in message, and awaits further instructions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device is remotely controlled for DDoS or brute-force attacks.

attack_chain.action: Bot binary decodes embedded credentials and attempts brute-force logins on other devices to propagate the infection.

behavioral_signatures: Remote code execution via web interface parameters (e.g., tools_ip_url, key) followed by immediate outbound HTTP requests to download scripts
Download and execution of shell scripts or binaries from untrusted IP addresses (e.g., 194.180.48.100)
Immediate and recursive deletion of system and temporary logs (/var/log/*, /tmp/*, /var/tmp/*) after infection
Automated modification of iptables/firewall rules to block common admin ports (SSH/Telnet)
Outbound connections to hardcoded C2 IPs (e.g., 194.180.48.101:5034) using custom protocols
Brute-force login attempts using known default credentials decoded from binary data
file_indicators: Presence of l.sh, i.sh, lolol.sh in /tmp or other writable directories
Downloaded binaries named bot.arm7, bot.mips, bot.x86, etc., in temporary directories
Unusual and immediate deletion of /var/log/*, /tmp/*, /var/tmp/* after exploit activity
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/S requests to 194.180.48.100, 2.56.59.215, 212.192.241.72 for script or binary downloads
C2 communication to 194.180.48.101:5034 using custom check-in messages
Unusual outbound traffic to external IPs immediately following exploit attempts or script execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for exploit attempts against known vulnerable device endpoints, especially web interface parameters. Detect and alert on outbound HTTP/S requests to known malicious IPs or the download and execution of shell scripts/binaries from untrusted sources. Watch for immediate and recursive log deletion and unauthorized firewall rule changes. Flag unsolicited outbound connections to hardcoded C2 IPs and brute-force login attempts originating from infected devices. Correlate these behaviors and indicators for high-confidence detection of Mirai/IZ1H9 infections, and prioritize response to devices exhibiting multiple indicators in sequence.
